title: Religious life
hook: poverty, chastity and obedience, lived in community

segments.voice: Yesterday, the single life: Paul's line that every one hath his proper gift, and room for the things of the Lord. Your line was a whole calling. Which single friend heard what you'd noticed? Day one thousand four hundred nine.

A young woman kneels in a chapel in front of her community: a row of women in the same habit, some of them old enough to be her grandmother. She holds a card. Her voice shakes a little as she reads from it. She is promising to own nothing of her own, to love no one as a spouse, and to go where she's sent. In some communities, she then lays the card on the altar and signs it there, in front of everyone. Afterward there's cake in the convent kitchen and her family taking photos. Her brother still doesn't quite get it. Today's word: evangelical counsels.
screen: `A CARD, READ ALOUD IN A CHAPEL.` → `NOTHING OWNED. NO SPOUSE. SENT.` → `SIGNED ON THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Evangelical here doesn't name a church. It means of the Gospel. The counsels are the Gospel's invitations, as opposed to its commands. The Catechism draws the line: the commandments are for everyone; the counsels point to ways of removing whatever, even if not wrong, gets in the way of love. It names them: poverty, chastity and obedience. Where do they come from? Take poverty. A rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me." The young man goes away sad, Matthew says, because he had a great deal. The counsel is the part he couldn't do. Chastity, for a religious, means celibacy: leaving marriage aside so that the heart is free for God and for everyone. Obedience means putting your own will into the hands of the community and its superior, as Jesus put his into the Father's. The Catechism says it's the profession of these counsels, in a stable state of life the Church recognizes, that marks consecrated life. And it's lived together. A religious sister or brother doesn't do this alone: they share a table, a rule, a chapel, and a superior who sends them. Not every community words the vows the same way. Benedict's Rule has a monk promise stability, faithfulness to the monastic way of life, and obedience, and Catholics read the same counsels inside it. Some orders add a vow of their own. The three run underneath.
screen: `EVANGELICAL: OF THE GOSPEL.` · `GO SELL WHAT THOU HAST.` · `POVERTY, CHASTITY, OBEDIENCE.` · `LIVED TOGETHER, UNDER A RULE.` · then, large: `AND COME FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for sisters and brothers. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a religious sister, brother, monk or nun you have known, or seen, or read about. A teacher, a nurse, someone at a soup kitchen, a monastery on a hill. Picture them at their ordinary work today. If you pray, you can ask God to keep them faithful and glad in their vows, and to send the people their communities need. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with thanks for one thing they gave away. The bell holds the time.
Evangelical counsels. The Gospel's invitations to poverty, chastity and obedience, which religious sisters and brothers profess as vows and live in community. Today's word.
Your line: three vows. Today, take a small share in one of them: give one thing away, or set aside one want, or let someone else choose this time. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholic religious sisters, brothers, monks and nuns profess vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, or a formula that contains them, after a time of formation, and live in community under a rule approved by the Church. Some communities profess an additional vow particular to their mission.

what it means: the Gospel's invitations to poverty, chastity and obedience, professed for life and lived in community.

what a scholar hears: the Catechism distinguishes the counsels from the precepts (CCC 1973) and defines consecrated life by their profession in a stable, Church-recognized state (CCC 915); Benedict's Rule, chapter 58, uses a different formula.

sources.quoted: If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 19:21: confirm. Verse 22 is paraphrased ('had a great deal') because the exact DR wording ('many possessions' / 'great possessions') wasn't certain.

CCC 915 (profession of the counsels within a permanent, Church-recognized state characterizes consecrated life) and CCC 1973 (counsels remove what hinders charity even if not contrary to it): paraphrased; confirm.
Benedictine vows (stability, conversatio morum, obedience) from the Rule, chapter 58: confirm the rendering 'faithfulness to the monastic way of life'.
'Some orders add a vow of their own' is unquantified; confirm.
Hook: signing the vow formula on the altar is given as a custom 'in some communities'; confirm.
Original: 'consilia evangelica', ecclesiastical Latin pronunciation; confirm.
